title: Tutelo & the Totteroy

bodyMarkdown:
The Tutelo (Yesáh in their own language) were an Eastern Siouan people, related to the Saponi and Occaneechi, who lived above the Fall Line in what is now Virginia and West Virginia (Wikipedia). Their name appears as “Totteroy” on the Big Sandy River, the Kentucky–West Virginia line, on British maps of 1755–76 (Evans, Mitchell, Pownall). Wikipedia says their homeland “was said to include” the Big Sandy and that the Iroquois dispersed them in the later Beaver Wars (c. 1670); Virginia Places says they “may have been living” near Williamson, West Virginia. Anthropologist James Griffin (1942) wrote that there is “no historic evidence that the Tutelo ever lived on the stream,” and suggested the name was perhaps due to the Walker and Gist exploring parties, or to the river serving as a route by which Ohio Valley peoples and the Iroquois could reach the Tutelo. The documented record starts in Virginia: in September 1671 the Batts and Fallam expedition left its horses with the Totero near present Radford on the New River (Encyclopedia Virginia), while Virginia Places thinks “Totero Town” was probably at Salem; the site is disputed. The Tutelo then joined the Saponi on the Roanoke River; in 1701 John Lawson found them on the Yadkin in North Carolina; after 1714 they lived near Fort Christanna in Brunswick County, Virginia (Wikipedia; NCpedia). The Cayuga adopted them in 1753, and their village Coreorgonel, near Ithaca, New York, was destroyed by the Sullivan Expedition in 1779; they then went to Canada (Wikipedia). Kentucky: A. Gwynn Henderson (1992) lists Tutelo among the groups known from mid-1700s eyewitness accounts of the Bluegrass and middle Ohio Valley, without naming a site. No source cited here documents a Tutelo village in Kentucky.
